texts.title: Why Do Leaves Change Colors in the Fall
texts.author: U.S. National Park Service
texts.license: U.S. federal government work; public domain in the U.S.
texts.length_note: full article excerpt
texts.central_idea: Trees drop their leaves and break down chlorophyll to save energy for winter, which reveals the other pigments already in the leaf.
supporting_details: Chlorophyll absorbs sunlight to make food and gives leaves their green color.
Shorter days and colder temperatures signal the tree to conserve energy.
The tree sends an enzyme to break down chlorophyll.
Other pigments become visible once chlorophyll is gone.
Rain and cool weather affect how bright the colors are.
texts.cautions: Source uses exclamation points; quote as written or trim. Define pigment, chlorophyll, and enzyme in context.

texts.title: Where is Earth's Water?
texts.author: U.S. Geological Survey, Water Science School
texts.license: U.S. federal government work; public domain in the U.S.
texts.length_note: prose excerpt; excludes data table
texts.cell_use: Owns main_idea_band_7_1_0002 and may supply other passages in that cell. Does not serve text_structure_band_7_1_0001: a work serves one cell only. Doubtful it yields 8 disjoint prose passages because the page is table-heavy.
texts.central_idea: Almost all of Earth's water is salt water or locked in ice and underground, so only a tiny share is fresh surface water that people can use.
supporting_details: About 96 percent of Earth's water is saline.
Over 68 percent of freshwater is in ice and glaciers.
About 30 percent of freshwater is underground.
Surface freshwater is about 1/150th of one percent of total water.
Rivers and lakes supply most of the water people use.
texts.cautions: Page is table-heavy; use the prose excerpt. Recheck figures at authoring time.

texts.title: The Diamond Necklace
texts.author: Guy de Maupassant
texts.license: Public domain in the U.S.
texts.length_note: full short story; excerpt required for one lesson
texts.central_idea: A young woman's desire for a richer life leads her to borrow a necklace, lose it, and spend years paying for a replacement that was never valuable.
supporting_details: Mathilde is unhappy with her ordinary life and wants to appear wealthy.
She borrows a necklace for the ball and loses it.
The couple borrows heavily to buy a replacement.
Years of hard work and poverty follow.
The ending reveals the original necklace was paste.
texts.cautions: 1884 and translated; violates the modern-text default below grade 11. Full story is too long for five items; excerpt must still contain setup, loss, and reveal.

texts.title: The Water in You: Water and the Human Body
texts.author: U.S. Geological Survey, Water Science School
texts.license: U.S. federal government work; public domain in the U.S.
texts.length_note: prose sections usable; FK measured on the opening sections, not the percentage tables
texts.fk_note: body FK 9.8 because of the percentage and citation paragraphs; the opening two sections measure 5.1 and 7.2
texts.slot_note: provisional slot: first inference lesson of Band 4.1
texts.single_passage_warning: Use prose only. Drop the percentage tables and the 1945 citation; they raise the readability score without adding inference work.
texts.central_idea: The share of water in the human body changes with age and body fat, and water is required for nearly every function the body performs.
supporting_details: Babies are born at about 78 percent water; by age one the share falls to about 65 percent.
Adult men are about 60 percent water; adult women are about 55 percent, because fat tissue holds less water than lean tissue.
The brain and heart are about 73 percent water and the lungs about 83 percent.
Even bones contain water, about 31 percent.
Water carries nutrients, removes waste, and controls body temperature.
texts.cautions: The page mixes simple prose with percent tables and a citation. Excerpt only the prose.

texts.title: What is a rip current?
texts.author: NOAA National Ocean Service
texts.license: U.S. federal government work; public domain in the U.S.
texts.length_note: short page; supports one lesson of two parts, not a cell
texts.slot_note: provisional slot: second inference lesson of Band 4.1
texts.single_passage_warning: One paragraph scores 14.0 because of words like prevalent and channels. Rewrite nothing, but do not build an item on that sentence alone.
texts.central_idea: A rip current is a fast, narrow flow moving away from shore, and swimmers get into trouble by fighting it instead of swimming parallel to the beach.
supporting_details: Rip currents occur on the East, Gulf, and West coasts and in the Great Lakes.
They move up to eight feet per second, faster than an Olympic swimmer.
A rip current is not the same thing as a rip tide.
The way out is to swim parallel to shore rather than against the current.
texts.cautions: Very short. Pair it with a second work if the cell needs more than one lesson from this topic.

texts.title: Dehydration
texts.author: MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine
texts.license: U.S. federal government work; public domain in the U.S.
texts.length_note: definition and cause paragraphs usable; the at-risk list drives the page-level score
texts.fk_note: page-level 8.5 is inflated by the list of chronic illnesses; the definition paragraphs measure about 5
texts.slot_note: provisional slot: third inference lesson of Band 4.1
texts.single_passage_warning: Excerpt the prose only. The at-risk list carries diabetes, cystic fibrosis, and kidney problems, which are outside grade-4 knowledge.
texts.central_idea: Dehydration happens when a person loses more fluid than they take in, and some people are at higher risk because their bodies signal thirst weakly or lose fluid faster.
supporting_details: Dehydration is a loss of too much fluid from the body.
It happens when fluid loss exceeds fluid intake.
Some older adults lose their sense of thirst as they age.
Infants and young children dehydrate faster because of diarrhea or vomiting.
Some medicines and illnesses cause more urination or sweating.
texts.cautions: Strip the site banner and the terminology notice before banking a passage. The at-risk list is a knowledge barrier at this band.

texts.title: Caves and Aquifers
texts.author: U.S. National Park Service
texts.license: U.S. federal government work; public domain in the U.S.
texts.placement_note: Measured 7.7 at its densest paragraph and 4.5 at its simplest; idea load is one-step, so 1.2.1 places it one band below its language score.
texts.length_note: prose sections usable
texts.slot_note: provisional slot: fourth inference lesson of Band 4.1
texts.single_passage_warning: karst, porosity, aquifer, and soluble are above the band. Each must be supported in help[0] or tell, per 1.2.1.
texts.central_idea: Caves form when slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolves bedrock, and the same openings can hold groundwater like a sponge.
supporting_details: Rain picks up carbon dioxide from the air and soil, which makes it slightly acidic.
Slightly acidic water dissolves bedrock over a long time, which opens caves.
Porous rock acts like a sponge and stores groundwater.
The openings in cave country store a large share of the groundwater people use.
texts.cautions: The page addresses the reader in a light voice in places. Keep the tone adult; do not copy 'Don't worry though!' into student copy.

texts.title: What Is a Black Hole? (Grades 5-8)
texts.author: National Aeronautics and Space Administration
texts.license: U.S. federal government work; public domain in the U.S.
texts.placement_note: Dense paragraphs run to 9+; the explanatory paragraphs about mass and gravity measure 5.1 and 6.7. Placement uses those, per 1.2.1.
texts.length_note: use the mass-and-gravity sections only
texts.slot_note: provisional slot: fifth inference lesson of Band 4.1
texts.single_passage_warning: Skip the singularity and event-horizon paragraphs; they are far above the band and are not needed for the inference.
texts.central_idea: A black hole pulls with the gravity of whatever mass it holds, so one with the sun's mass would keep the planets in their orbits, and the sun itself is too small to become one.
supporting_details: A black hole with the same mass as the sun would have the same gravity as the sun.
Earth would not fall in; the planets would orbit it the same way.
The sun does not have enough mass to collapse into a black hole.
At the end of its life the sun will become a red giant and throw off its outer layers.
texts.cautions: The page is written for students, so its framing is school-facing. The passage is fine; the tutor must not adopt a classroom voice.

texts.title: The Story of the Beaver Marsh
texts.author: U.S. National Park Service
texts.license: U.S. federal government work; public domain in the U.S.
texts.length_note: three adapted passages, 100-103 words each
texts.central_idea: A wetland that was drained and junked came back after volunteers cleared the junk and beavers raised the water.
supporting_details: Land development and the Ohio and Erie Canal drained the original wetland.
A dairy farm, homes, and an auto repair shop stood on the land by the 1970s.
Beavers returned in the late 1970s after more than a century away and built dams that flooded the area.
Sierra Club volunteers and the park service hauled away car parts, bed springs, and trash in the mid 1980s.
Ohio has lost nearly 90 percent of its wetlands, and 46 percent of endangered species need wetlands.
texts.cautions: Local names (Lock 26, Howe Meadow, Riverview Road) were kept; they date the place without adding difficulty. Recheck the two percentages at authoring time.

texts.title: Shenandoah: Not Without the CCC
texts.author: U.S. National Park Service
texts.license: U.S. federal government work; public domain in the U.S.
texts.length_note: three adapted passages, 101-108 words each
texts.central_idea: CCC crews built the park's roads, buildings, and views, so much of what looks wild was made by people.
supporting_details: Two CCC camps opened in 1933, and ten stood in or near the park by 1942.
The Army ran the camps; the National Park Service chose the work.
Crews built trails, fire roads, comfort stations, a sawmill, a shingle mill, a blacksmith shop, and nurseries.
Crews cleared, planted, and shaped the land along the Skyline Drive.
Researchers say no area in view of the drive is fully natural.
texts.cautions: Needs one line of context for the Depression, which the passage supplies. The 1933 pageant quotation was dropped.

texts.title: The Water Cycle
texts.author: U.S. Geological Survey, Water Science School
texts.license: U.S. federal government work; public domain in the U.S.
texts.length_note: three adapted passages, 100-104 words each
texts.central_idea: Water is always moving between the places it is stored, and people change that movement.
supporting_details: Water is stored in the air, on the land, and below the ground, as liquid, solid, or gas.
Oceans hold about 96 percent of Earth's water; the rest is fresh.
Pools hold water for very different lengths of time.
Water moves by evaporation, clouds, rain, runoff, and underground flow.
People pump water, build dams, drain wetlands, and change how clean the water is.
texts.cautions: Strip the diagram labels and the linked-page references. Do not import the 68/30 percent figures; they belong to a different USGS page.

texts.title: Wildland Fire: What is a Prescribed Fire?
texts.author: U.S. National Park Service
texts.license: U.S. federal government work; public domain in the U.S.
texts.length_note: three adapted passages, 102-107 words each
texts.central_idea: A prescribed fire is a planned burn held to written conditions and used to reach a goal on the land.
supporting_details: A prescription covers public and crew safety, weather, and the chance of meeting the goal.
Burns clear fuel near homes, create habitat, help rare species, and keep historic scenes open.
Every burn needs a fire management plan and a burn plan.
A go/no-go list is checked on the day of the burn.
When fire cannot be used, crews cut and haul brush and may burn the piles later.
texts.cautions: Drop the ignition-device chemistry (glycol, potassium permanganate) and the park statistics. Keep the two park examples as examples only.

texts.title: Hurricanes
texts.author: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
texts.license: U.S. federal government work; public domain in the U.S.
texts.length_note: three adapted passages, 100-102 words each
texts.central_idea: A hurricane is a storm fed by warm ocean water, and storms are sorted by wind speed and named by the place where they form.
supporting_details: Hurricanes are low-pressure systems that gain energy from warm ocean water.
Winds circle in closed circulation around a calm eye, with the eyewall around it.
Storms are classed by wind speed: below 39, 39-73, and 74 miles per hour and above.
Storms need warm water, moist air, and steady winds to grow.
The same storm is a hurricane, a typhoon, or a cyclone depending on where it forms, and names are reused every six years.
texts.cautions: The page is navigation-heavy; extract the three sections only. Coriolis and wind shear were dropped as above the band.

texts.title: What is a planet?
texts.author: National Aeronautics and Space Administration
texts.license: U.S. federal government work; public domain in the U.S.
texts.length_note: three adapted passages, 101-105 words each
texts.central_idea: The word planet means what astronomers agree it means, and that agreement changed when new objects were found.
supporting_details: The 2006 definition requires a planet to orbit a star, be round from its own gravity, and clear its path.
Pluto was called the ninth planet from 1930.
Better telescopes found many icy objects in the Kuiper Belt in the 1990s.
Eris, found in 2005, forced the vote that made Pluto a dwarf planet.
Astronomers still disagree about the rule, and the meaning may change again.
texts.cautions: Highest idea load in the rung: the subject is a definition, not an object. Keep the disagreement, or the passage teaches a false certainty.

texts.title: The Field That Rests
texts.author: Written for this lesson
texts.license: Original text, written for this lesson
texts.length_note: three passages, one per displayed part
texts.cell_use: Owns its own lesson in main_idea Band 4.3 and serves no other cell. Drafted for the band, so it yields no second passage beyond its three parts.
texts.central_idea: A farmer gives up a season of income so the field can rebuild what repeated cropping took out.
supporting_details: A fallow field is planted with a cover crop, and none of it is sold.
Repeated cropping takes nitrogen out, builds pests and weeds, and lets rain carry soil away.
Legumes store nitrogen in their roots; the cover shades weeds; roots feed soil life.
The gain arrives later, as less fertilizer and a bigger next crop.
A cover crop between cash crops keeps money coming in but does not rest the ground the same way.
texts.cautions: No yield or price figures. The economics stay qualitative on purpose.
texts.text_status: Drafted for the band, review pending.

texts.title: The Word That Changed Its Mind
texts.author: Written for this lesson
texts.license: Original text, written for this lesson
texts.length_note: three passages, one per displayed part
texts.cell_use: Owns its own lesson in main_idea Band 4.3 and serves no other cell. Drafted for the band, so it yields no second passage beyond its three parts.
texts.central_idea: Word meanings drift through everyday use, and dictionaries record the drift rather than decide it.
supporting_details: Nice came from Latin nescius, meant foolish in the 1200s, exact in the 1500s, and pleasant by 1700.
No one voted; speakers used the word in new ways and listeners followed.
Awful moved the other way, from full of awe to bad.
A dictionary records senses already in common use and keeps old ones until they die out.
texts.cautions: Etymologies are the standard reference ones, stated without fine dates. Do not add a dictionary citation.
texts.text_status: Drafted for the band, review pending.

texts.title: The Price Before Dawn
texts.author: Written for this lesson
texts.license: Original text, written for this lesson
texts.length_note: three passages, one per displayed part
texts.cell_use: Owns its own lesson in main_idea Band 4.3 and serves no other cell. Drafted for the band, so it yields no second passage beyond its three parts.
texts.central_idea: The day's price is found on the market floor from that morning's supply, and it lasts about a day.
supporting_details: Nothing is marked; the seller quotes a price when a buyer stops.
A glut lowers the price, and a short load raises it.
A seller would rather sell cheap than hold a crate worth nothing by morning.
Weather two weeks earlier reaches the price only through the size of today's load.
Tomorrow's price is found again, from a different set of trucks.
texts.cautions: No market name, city, or figures. The practice is described generally.
texts.text_status: Drafted for the band, review pending.

texts.title: Twenty-Six Miles and Change
texts.author: Written for this lesson
texts.license: Original text, written for this lesson
texts.length_note: three passages, one per displayed part
texts.cell_use: Owns its own lesson in main_idea Band 4.3 and serves no other cell. Drafted for the band, so it yields no second passage beyond its three parts.
texts.central_idea: A race distance that came from one 1908 course was later fixed by agreement for every marathon.
supporting_details: The 1908 race started below Windsor Castle and finished in a west London stadium.
The finish moved in front of the royal box, which added 385 yards.
Later host cities chose their own distances, so times could not be compared.
In 1921 the world running body adopted the London figure as the standard.
The odd tail of the race still shapes how runners plan a finish.
texts.cautions: No times, records, or runner names; each would need verification and none is needed.

texts.title: The Village Under the Water
texts.author: Written for this lesson
texts.license: Original text, written for this lesson
texts.length_note: three passages, one per displayed part
texts.cell_use: Owns its own lesson in main_idea Band 4.3 and serves no other cell. Drafted for the band, so it yields no second passage beyond its three parts.
texts.central_idea: A reservoir is built by emptying a lived-in valley, and the place stays half-visible under the water.
supporting_details: A river valley with high sides and a narrow end is dammed to hold water.
The land is bought, sometimes under a law that allows taking it.
Some buildings are sold or reused; a stone church keeps its walls because removal costs too much.
Graves are moved because families ask and because a drowned cemetery is a public problem.
In a dry summer the walls, the road, and a bridge come back into view.
texts.cautions: No town, valley, reservoir, or date is named. Naming a real one would require facts this text does not carry.

texts.title: The Pass That Closes for Winter
texts.author: Written for this lesson
texts.license: Original text, written for this lesson
texts.length_note: three passages, one per displayed part
texts.cell_use: Owns its own lesson in main_idea Band 4.3 and serves no other cell. Drafted for the band, so it yields no second passage beyond its three parts.
texts.central_idea: Some mountain passes close on purpose, because a slide cannot be managed while traffic is on the road.
supporting_details: Crews fire charges to bring snow down at an hour they choose, then plow the road.
A loaded slope can release without warning, and a car under it has nowhere to go.
Closing removes what would be hurt and lets crews work on their own schedule.
The cost falls on the towns: longer drives, rerouted deliveries, a thinner clinic.
A tunnel or gallery keeps a pass open, but costs far more than a gate.
texts.cautions: No pass, highway, or agency is named. Drive times are illustrative, not measured.
texts.text_status: Drafted for the band, review pending.

texts.title: The Tree That Keeps Its Leaves
texts.author: Written for this lesson
texts.license: Original text, written for this lesson
texts.length_note: three passages, one per displayed part
texts.cell_use: Owns its own lesson in vocab Band 3.1 and serves no other cell. Drafted for the band, so it yields no second passage beyond its three parts.
texts.central_idea: Evergreens keep their leaves because a narrow, waxy needle holds water on days when a wide leaf cannot.
supporting_details: A pine's thin, sharp leaves are called needles.
Winter freezes the ground water, so a tree cannot replace what it loses.
A waxy coat and a small surface keep water loss low.
A narrow needle and a cone shape shed snow before a branch breaks.
The tree drops a few old needles at a time, so the branch never looks bare.
texts.cautions: No species named beyond pine and maple. No needle counts or year spans.
texts.text_status: Drafted for the band, review pending.

texts.title: The Lighthouse Keeper's Night
texts.author: Written for this lesson

texts.central_idea: A keeper's night was a few small tasks repeated, and the lens was what turned one flame into a light ships could see.
supporting_details: The wick is the cord that draws oil into the flame.
A long wick smokes, so the keeper trims it with scissors.
The lens bends the flame into a beam that reaches twenty miles.
The keeper checks oil, logs passing ships, and rings the bell in fog.
texts.cautions: No lighthouse, country, or date. No ship counts or pay figures.

texts.author: Written for this lesson
texts.license: Original text, written for this lesson

texts.central_idea: Bread rises because yeast eats sugar and gives off gas the dough traps, so the baker's job is warmth and time.
supporting_details: Yeast is a living thing that gives off gas.
The gas forms bubbles, and the dough swells and lifts.
Warmth helps the yeast; too much heat kills it.
Pressing and folding the dough clears big bubbles and lines up the strands.
In the oven the gas expands once more before the crust sets.
texts.cautions: No temperatures, times, or flour amounts. No brand or region.
texts.text_status: Drafted for the band, review pending.

texts.title: The Cobbler's Bench
texts.author: Written for this lesson
texts.license: Original text, written for this lesson
texts.length_note: three passages, one per displayed part
texts.cell_use: Owns its own lesson in vocab Band 3.1 and serves no other cell. Drafted for the band, so it yields no second passage beyond its three parts.
texts.central_idea: A cobbler's repair is shaped by the shoe: the sole keeps water out, the form keeps the shape, and the short stitch keeps the patch.
supporting_details: The sole is the bottom of a shoe, and a worn sole lets rain reach the foot.
A wooden form holds the shoe's shape while wet leather dries.
A drawer of buckles and laces lets a customer buy a part, not a pair.
Few shoes are mended now, because new shoes cost less than a repair.
texts.cautions: No prices, dates, or place names. No claim about how many cobblers remain.

texts.title: The Race Nobody Wins Early
texts.author: Written for this lesson
texts.license: Original text, written for this lesson

texts.cell_use: Owns its own lesson in vocab Band 3.1 and serves no other cell. Drafted for the band, so it yields no second passage beyond its three parts.
texts.central_idea: A long race is won by saving speed for the end, and the same limit applies to a month of study.
supporting_details: A pace is a speed a runner can hold for the whole distance.
Steady means an even speed, not the fastest speed.
A sprint is a short burst the body cannot keep up.
A runner who saved strength can answer a tired runner's finish.
texts.cautions: No distances, times, or named runners. No training claims.

texts.author: Written for this lesson

texts.central_idea: A sign painter's skill shows in spacing and patience rather than in the drawing alone.
supporting_details: An outline around each letter makes the shape stand out.
The painter rests his wrist so the line does not shake.
The first coat is thin and soaks into the wood.
A coat put on wet makes the sign blister in the sun.
A hard-to-read sign is usually crowded, not badly drawn.

texts.author: Written for this lesson

texts.central_idea: Hand-set printing worked because the type was reversed, a second reader checked it, and the press took one sheet at a time.
supporting_details: One metal block stands for each letter, cut in reverse.
The apprentice sets lines without looking, keeping his eyes on the copy.
A proofreader catches the reversed letters the setter has stopped seeing.
Presswork ran about a hundred sheets an hour, and paper was dear.
Setting still took one letter at a time, and the type was taken apart after.

texts.title: The River That Bends
texts.author: Written for this lesson
texts.license: Original text, written for this lesson
texts.length_note: three passages, one per displayed part
texts.cell_use: Owns its own lesson in vocab Band 4.1 and serves no other cell. Drafted for the band, so it yields no second passage beyond its three parts.
texts.central_idea: A river's bend is the shape moving water gives to soil: the outside loses ground, the inside gains it, and a loop may be cut off as an oxbow.
supporting_details: Fast water on the outside of a bend carries soil away.
Slow water on the inside drops silt and builds a shelf.
A loop cut off from the river becomes an oxbow lake.
Engineers stone the outside bank but rarely straighten a river, because fast water floods worse.
texts.cautions: No river, region, or measurement. No rate for how fast a bend moves.

texts.title: The Whistle That Waits
texts.author: Written for this lesson
texts.license: Original text, written for this lesson

texts.central_idea: The referee's whistle is a tool for restoring fair play, so it waits when stopping play would hurt the team that was fouled.
supporting_details: A foul is contact such as a push, a trip, or a hand on the ball.
A foul usually stops play and gives the ball to the other team.
Stopping play can take away the fouled team's best chance.
Playing the advantage is a judgment, and the wait is short because injury is a risk.
Coaches teach players to stay up through a light push.
texts.cautions: No sport, league, or referee is named. No rule numbers or penalty distances.

texts.central_idea: A one-room school taught students at different levels by rotating recitation groups, and its calendar bent around the harvest.
supporting_details: One teacher taught every grade in a single room.
Recitation meant saying the lesson aloud from memory.
Slates were wiped clean, and paper was saved for a final copy.
Monitor duty was a student hearing the younger ones read.
A term ran between harvests, and pay could depend on attendance.

texts.author: Written for this lesson

texts.central_idea: Salt preserved meat by removing the water bacteria need, and the cost of salt decided what each region ate in winter.
supporting_details: Meat was packed in dry salt or soaked in brine.
Salt pulls water out, and spoiling bacteria cannot grow without it.
A hard rind protects the cured meat from mold and insects.
Smoke added flavor but the salt did the preserving.
Where salt was dear, regions dried or buried food instead.

texts.central_idea: Editing removes what stands between the reader and the thought, and the best editing is answered mark by mark rather than obeyed.

Spare means no decoration, not short.
The hardest cut is a good sentence in the wrong place.
Tightening keeps the argument and shortens the sentences.
The editor sees the shape; the writer knows which detail is load-bearing.
A draft survives when every mark is answered by a change or a reason.

texts.central_idea: Fungi break dead matter back into circulation and trade with living roots, which is why the soil is literally alive.

Leftover material stays in the soil and is taken up by plants.
Decomposition returns material to circulation rather than merely rotting it.
A fungus trades water and minerals for sugar from a tree's roots.
The mushroom is the fruit; the web in the soil is most of the organism.

texts.central_idea: Stock is money already spent, so waiting on the shelf costs twice: the goods lose value and the cash cannot move.

Margin is the gap between cost and selling price.
A small margin on a fast item can beat a large margin on a slow one.
Spoilage is the visible loss, and markdowns erase the margin.
The same cash cannot buy what is selling, so the cost is paid twice.

supporting_details: The count decides representation and money for a place.
A household is everyone under one roof, related or not.
A taker may not guess, so doubtful answers are recorded as given.
A house was visited three times before it could be recorded as empty.
A return is the filed sheet, and its value depends on consistent treatment.

texts.central_idea: A heavy apple crop spends the energy next year's buds need, so growers thin the fruit to break the cycle.
supporting_details: Many varieties swing between a heavy year and a light one.
Next spring's buds form in the summer of the heavy crop.
A tree carrying heavy fruit cannot make strong buds, so the next crop is light.
Thinning removes young fruit in early summer so the rest grow larger.
The harvest lost this year is paid back next year, and the two-year total is usually higher.
texts.cautions: No variety names, yields, or prices. No claim about which regions grow which apples.

The rider behind the front wheel uses less effort at speed.
A line of riders moves faster than any single rider in it.

Cold-climate seeds often will not start until they have been through a winter.
Growers copy a winter by keeping seed cold in damp sand before sowing.
The trigger is the return of warmth after a long cold, not the cold alone.
One warm week in midwinter does not start a seed.

The water changes both the depth and the ramp.

texts.central_idea: Water in a sidewalk crack freezes, expands, and pushes the crack wider, and tar stops it by keeping water out.

At night the water freezes into ice.
Ice takes more room than water, so it pushes the crack apart.
The freeze repeats night after night, and the crack widens a little each time.
Tar keeps water out, so there is nothing left to freeze and push.

texts.central_idea: A painted cloth backdrop cracked because the paint shrank as it dried fast while the cloth did not, and the crew fixed it by slowing the drying.
supporting_details: The backdrop was painted on cloth and hung above the stage.
The room was warm and dry, so the paint dried too fast.
The paint shrank as it dried, and the cloth did not shrink with it.
Small cracks opened and spread to the middle by opening night.
The crew painted a thin new layer and let it dry slowly in a cool room.

texts.central_idea: An ice harvest ran in a fixed order because each position had its own reason: snow was cleared so the ice could thicken, the surface was scored so the saw had a line, blocks were packed at once so they did not melt, and the crew cut in January because late ice is thin and soft.
supporting_details: Snow blankets the ice and keeps it from growing, so the crew cleared it first.
Scoring the surface came before cutting, because the shallow lines guided every later stroke.
Each block was floated to a ramp and hauled up by horses.
The blocks were packed in sawdust inside a windowless ice house, which slowed the melting.
Ice cut in March is thinner and softer than ice cut in January, so the month decided how much work paid.
texts.why_it_works: A five-step seasonal chain in which four positions each carry a separate reason; the last item joins the month to the yield.
texts.cautions: No town, company, price, or date. No claim about who bought the ice.

texts.central_idea: A dam's removal led to a rush of silt and a slow river repair: the gravel was clean by the third year and the fish returned in the fourth, so the first summer looked like failure and the fifth like success.
supporting_details: The dam held silt, sand, and leaves behind it, and fish could not reach the gravel.
The first year after removal brought trapped silt downstream onto the gravel beds.
Neighbors saw brown water and bare banks and concluded the removal had failed.
Each spring flood moved some silt, and by the third year the stones were scoured and bright.
Fish arrived in the fourth spring, after the gravel was clean.
texts.why_it_works: A delayed effect chain: one action, three effects that arrive on different clocks, and a reader who must keep their order apart.

texts.central_idea: A barge and a truck differ on load, speed, and cost per ton, and neither wins outright: the choice depends on whether a shipment can wait for the cheap slow way or must arrive by a date.
supporting_details: One barge tow carries as much grain as sixty trucks, with a crew of three.
A barge takes five days, cannot leave the water, and stops when the river freezes.
A truck loads in an hour and drives all night.
A barge costs less per ton because fuel and crew are spread across a much larger load.
Grain that must meet a ship goes by truck, because a late barge is worse than a costly one.
texts.why_it_works: A three-dimension comparison that refuses to name a winner; the decisive dimension is the shipment's timing.

texts.central_idea: A track's puddle was first treated with sand, which worked for a month and moved the water; the real cause was a root-blocked drain pipe, so the successful first fix hid the fault it never touched.
supporting_details: After heavy rain a shallow lake stood on the far curve for two days.
The sand filled the small holes in the surface, so water ran off the curve.
The water pooled at the low end of the straight, which had never been wet.
Roots from a line of trees had closed the drain pipe to the width of a thumb.
The crew cut the roots, replaced the pipe, and dug a channel to the ditch.
texts.why_it_works: A problem/solution where the first solution partly works, which is harder than a plain wrong guess: the early success hides the cause.

The engineer measured the room with a clap and timed the echo at almost two seconds.

The room went dead, and players could not hear each other across the stage.

texts.central_idea: Fog forms in two ways, and a two-question test, clear sky and still air, sorts a case into the kind and says what the fog will do next.
supporting_details: The first kind forms on a clear, calm night, when the ground loses its heat and the air above it cannot hold its water.
The second kind forms when warm, wet air slides over a cold surface, so the air is moving and the ground need not cool.
Fog of the first kind burns off within hours of sunrise, while fog of the second kind thickens through the morning.
The test the weather service uses asks whether the sky is clear and whether the air is still, not what the temperature is.
Two places with the same temperature at six in the morning were sorted into different kinds by the sky and the wind.

texts.central_idea: Kitchen scraps break down in a pile, become humus, feed a crop, and return to the kitchen as scraps, so the bin is one stage of a loop rather than an ending.
supporting_details: Bacteria breaking the scraps down give off heat, which is why the middle of the pile is warm.
A cold pile is too dry or too wet, and it needs a turn with a fork.
Turning puts the outside in, so air reaches material that had none and the pile heats a second time.
Humus holds water in sandy ground and loosens clay, and the worms carry it down into the bed.
The grower spreads the humus, the harvest comes back through the door, and the next scraps are the same material a year later.

texts.central_idea: A second packing table was ruled out before it was bought, because a narrow doorway fed the tables and the check station held the line.

Money spent on the table would have looked like progress on the books.

texts.title: The Verb in the Middle
texts.author: Written for this lesson
texts.license: Original text, written for this lesson
texts.length_note: three passages, one per displayed part (104, 105, 102 words)
texts.cell_use: Owns its own lesson in text_structure Band 4.2 and serves no other cell. Drafted for the band, so it yields no passage beyond its three parts.
texts.central_idea: The advice to keep sentences short survives only in part: where the verb sits and where the news arrives decide how hard a sentence is, and length is only a signal.
supporting_details: Writing guides say short sentences are easier, so cut a sentence in two.
A reader holds a subject in mind and waits for the verb that says what the subject did.
The long example gives the news after three words, and the shorter one saves it for the last moment.
A counter that rates the shorter sentence easier is counting length, which is a signal of difficulty and not the difficulty.
The advice that survives is to cut a sentence that is doing two jobs, not one that is long.
texts.why_it_works: A correction: the belief, the counter-example, then the narrower rule that survives; the reader has to see which part of the advice is kept.
texts.cautions: No study, journal, author, or date. No claim that length never matters.

texts.title: Rings Around the Square
texts.author: Written for this lesson
texts.license: Original text, written for this lesson
texts.length_note: three passages, one per displayed part (102, 108, 103 words)
texts.cell_use: Owns its own lesson in text_structure Band 4.2 and serves no other cell. Drafted for the band, so it yields no passage beyond its three parts.
texts.central_idea: A market town described in rings outward from its square is also described in centuries, so the plan of the place records the order in which it grew.
supporting_details: The first ring is shopfronts close to the square, with no room for gardens.
Beyond them the streets widen, then come small houses with long gardens, and last a road of garages and sheds.
Each ring was built in a different century, and the oldest is nearest the square.
The shopfronts came while carts used the square, the walled houses when the market moved to a covered hall, the gardens with the railway, the sheds with the vans.
A street directory lists streets alphabetically and cannot show how the town grew.
texts.why_it_works: A spatial order that carries chronology, so the reader reads distance as date; the closing comparison with a directory shows what the order is for.
texts.cautions: No town name, county, road name, or population. No street count beyond the four the passage states.

texts.title: The Rule With One Exception
texts.author: Written for this lesson
texts.license: Original text, written for this lesson
texts.length_note: three passages, one per displayed part (100, 103, 108 words)
texts.cell_use: Owns its own lesson in text_structure Band 4.2 and serves no other cell. Drafted for the band, so it yields no passage beyond its three parts.
texts.central_idea: The higher team hosts the final unless the grounds are more than four hundred miles apart, and the league keeps that line narrow because a rule with many exceptions settles nothing.
supporting_details: The team that finished higher in the table hosts, and the host is named before the season ends.
The travel and the strange changing room give the home side an edge.
Above four hundred miles the final is played at a neutral site between the grounds.
The exception was added after a visiting side left at five in the morning and lost to a team it had beaten twice.
Below the line the rule stands, because a rule with a hundred exceptions is no rule.
texts.why_it_works: A general rule with one written exception and a case that justifies its width, so the structure is the boundary between them.
texts.cautions: No club, league name, city, or score beyond the four goals the passage states. No player or coach named.
